title: Proceedings 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming
abstract: Since the first conference in Marseille in 1982, the International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP) has been the premier international event for presenting research in logic programming. These proceedings include the Technical Communications of the 42nd ICLP, held 20-23 July 2026 as part of FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The papers and extended abstracts in this volume address the following areas and topics: theoretical foundations, language design and programming methodologies, program analysis and optimization, applications and implementation methodologies. This volume features contributions to two submission tracks of ICLP 2026: the Main track and the Recently Published Research track.

Chudziak 529 Preface Since the first conference in Marseille in 1982, the International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP) has been the premier international event for presenting research in logic programming. These proceedings include the Technical Communications and Recently Published Research papers of the 42nd International Conference on Logic Programming (ICLP 2026) , held in Lisbon, Portugal, from July 20 to 23, 2026, as part of the Federated Logic Conference (FLoC) 2026 . The papers and extended abstracts in this volume address the following areas and topics: theoretical foundations, language design and programming methodologies, program analysis and optimization, applications and implementation methodologies. This volume features contributions to two submission tracks of ICLP 2026: the Main and Recently Published Research tracks. The ICLP 2026 Technical Communications include two types of contributions: regular papers and extended abstracts. Five contributions, which were contributed to the Recently Published Research track, describe published work that has not yet been presented at ICLP or other main conferences related to logic programming (such as LPNMR, LOPSTR, or LPAR). The remaining contributions present original research. Differently from the part of the ICLP 2026 proceedings published in a special issue of Theory and Practice of Logic Programming , these contributions have been directly submitted to the Technical Communications, comparable to short (regular) papers, or were considered as high-quality, yet still work in progress by the reviewers. In fact, the impact of ICLP Technical Communications is witnessed, e.g., by the 10 Years Test of Time Award of ICLP 2024 for the Technical Communications paper “ Clingo = ASP + Control: Preliminary Report ”. All contributions to the ICLP 2026 Technical Communications have been evaluated by three reviewers and were presented during ICLP 2026. This volume orders the Technical Communications and Recently Published Research papers following the planned ICLP 2026 program . New Encodings of the (Euclidean) Traveling Salesperson Problem in Constraint Answer Set Programming on Difference Logic Alessandro Bertagnon ( University of Ferrara ) Marco Gavanelli ( University of Ferrara ) Original Contribution Alessandro Bertagnon, Marco Gavanelli. New encodings of the (Euclidean) travelling salesperson problem in constraint answer set programming on difference logic. Journal of Logic and Computation 36(2) (2026). URL: https://doi.org/10.1093/logcom/exaf072 Keywords: Constraint Answer Set Programming, Travelling Salesperson Problem. Statement This submission is based on a previous paper presented at ASPOCP 2023 and also presented informally at CILC 2024 (39th Italian Conference on Computational Logic). This extended abstract refers to the publication in the Journal of Logic and Computation, which is a significantly extended and extensively revised version of the ASPOCP publication: it proposes new encodings to solve the TSP in clingo[DL]; such encodings were not present in the CILC and ASPOCP versions. Extended Abstract Introduction The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) is a fundamental problem where a salesperson must visit a set of nodes exactly once, minimizing total distance [ 1 ]. A particularly important class is the Euclidean TSP, where nodes correspond to points in the plane and distances are Euclidean. Although this variant remains NP-hard, it exposes additional geometric structure that can be exploited algorithmically. While the TSP is NP-hard, specialized solvers like Concorde [ 1 ] are highly efficient but lack the flexibility to handle "side constraints" common in real-life routing, such as time windows or capacity limits [ 1 ]. To address these, declarative techniques like Answer Set Programming (ASP) and Constraint Answer Set Programming (CASP) can be used [ 5 , 7 ]. We focus on clingo[DL] [ 6 ], which integrates Difference Logic to enable efficient propagation algorithms. Background A CASP program $\Pi$ is an ASP program in which the head of rules can also be a special atom $C$ called a constraint ; more precisely, a CASP program is built on a set of atoms $\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{L}$ where $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of regular atoms while $\mathcal{L}$ is the set of constraint atoms [ 6 ]. Regular atoms correspond to those used in standard ASP programs and their meaning is defined in the logic program. The meaning of the constraint atoms is defined in an external theory $\mathcal{T}$. Given a ground set of constraint atoms $\mathcal{S}$, a solution is an assignment of numeric values to the numeric variables such that all the constraints in $\mathcal{S}$ are satisfied in $\mathcal{T}$. For example, the atom 3*x <= 7 can be interpreted in the theory of linear equations over integers, and one solution is that the numeric variable x takes value 1. In clingo[DL], the theory atoms are of the form $x-y\leq c$, where $x,y$ are variables and $c$ is a constant [ 6 ]. Proposed Encodings We propose several encodings for the TSP using Difference Logic: the baseline is the encoding in [ 8 ], with the added Triangular inequality (SDLT) to speedup the search in Euclidean instances; the second is the DL encoding with Exit Bound (DLEB) : with respect to SDLT it uses a different way to compute the summation of the costs in the objective function, that lets one impose bounds on the minimum cost necessary to exit from each node of the graph; the third, named DL encoding with Dynamic Bound on first cost (DLDB1) , is able to update the bound when an edge having a low cost is excluded from the TSP; the DL encoding with Dynamic Bound (DLDB) generalizes DLDB1, while Compact DL encoding with Dynamic Bound (CDLDB) tries to reduce the memory required for the ground program. Additional technical details are available in the journal version [ 4 ]. Furthermore, we extend the proposed encodings to the Euclidean case by exploiting the property that an optimal Euclidean tour cannot intersect itself and must follow the order of nodes on the convex hull [ 2 , 3 ]. Experimental Evaluation We conducted experiments on randomly generated instances and the plot in Figure 1 highlights a strong performance improvement of the proposed DL-based encodings over SDLT. As shown with the logarithmic scale, most points lie well below the diagonal, indicating that the new encodings consistently outperform the baseline, often by several orders of magnitude. In particular, in a significant number of instances SDLT times out, while the proposed approaches are able to solve the same instances in a very short time, often within a few seconds. Although the current evaluation is limited to randomly generated benchmarks, these experiments provide evidence that the proposed techniques scale significantly better than previous CASP encodings. The compact variant CDLDB was specifically designed to reduce the grounding size and memory footprint, even if a more detailed empirical analysis of memory is left for future work. Figure 1: Experimental comparison of encodings. Conclusion Our results push the state of the art in CASP-based routing: the new encodings obtained impressive speedups of three orders of magnitude, enabling several instances that previously required over half an hour to be solved within seconds. The full journal version [ 4 ] provides additional technical details and a broader discussion of related TSP solution approaches. References David Applegate, Robert E. Relational Programming in Rel Molham Aref ( RelationalAI ) Paolo Guagliardo ( University of Edinburgh ) George Kastrinis ( RelationalAI ) Leonid Libkin ( RelationalAI & Univ of Edinburgh ) Victor Marsault ( LIGM, Univ. Gustave Eiffel, CNRS ) Wim Martens ( RelationalAI & University of Bayreuth ) Mary McGrath ( RelationalAI ) Filip Murlak ( University of Warsaw ) Nathaniel Nystrom ( RelationalAI ) Liat Peterfreund ( Hebrew University ) Allison Rogers ( RelationalAI ) Cristina Sirangelo ( Université Paris Cité, CNRS, IRIF ) Domagoj Vrgoč ( Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile ) David Zhao ( RelationalAI ) Abdul Zreika ( RelationalAI ) From the moment of their inception, languages for relational data have been described as sublanguages embedded in a host programming language. Rel is a new relational language whose key design goal is to go beyond this paradigm with features that allow for programming in the large, making it possible to fully describe end to end application semantics. The core of Rel is Datalog with first-order queries in rule bodies; this is the principal relevance to ICLP. It is then extended with features that let it model the entire application semantics: variables that range over tuples and sets of tuples; abstraction, and application. With the new approach, we can model the semantics of entire enterprise applications relationally, which helps significantly reduce architecture complexity and avoid the well-known impedance mismatch problem. This paradigm shift is enabled by 50 years of database research, making it possible to revisit the sublanguage/host language paradigm, starting from the fundamental principles. The paper presents the main features of Rel: those that give it the power to express traditional query language operations and those that are designed to grow the language and allow programming in the large. The original paper on Rel appeared in SIGMOD 2025 under the title "Rel: A Programming Language for Relational Data". After receiving a SIGMOD Research Highlights Award, a shorter version under the current title was published in SIGMOD Record. Contrast Sequential Pattern Mining with Answer Set Solving Gioacchino Sterlicchio ( DMMM, Polytechnic University of Bari, Bari, Italy ) Francesca Alessandra Lisi ( DIB and CILA, University of Bari Aldo Moro, Bari, Italy ) Statement The following extended abstract refers to the article published in the Machine Learning journal ([ 9 ]). The submission has not been already presented at a major logic programming forum (such as earlier ICLP, LPNMR, LOPSTR, LPAR). Keywords Declarative pattern mining - Contrast sequential pattern mining - Answer set programming Main contributions The work presented in ([ 9 ]) concerns an application of Answer Set Programming (ASP) ([ 1 ]) in the field of Pattern Mining, thus contributing to the stream of research known as Declarative Pattern Mining ([ 5 ]). More precisely, it introduces the first ASP-based declarative approach to the Contrast Sequential Pattern Mining (CSPM) task, which is named MASS-CSP (Mining with Answer Set Solving - Contrast Sequential Patterns). CSPM combines sequential pattern mining (i.e., identifying frequent subsequences in a set of sequences) with contrast pattern mining (i.e., identifying statistically significant differences across distinct datasets) to uncover patterns that characterize specific classes ([ 2 ]). The MASS-CSP framework provides a concise and versatile ASP encoding that addresses the basic CSPM task as well as several advanced extensions. These extensions include the mining of condensed representations , such as closed and maximal patterns ([ 4 ]), which help mitigate the problem of pattern explosion by reducing the number of extracted patterns without losing significant information. Other extensions are the gap and span constraints, typically used when mining sequential data to limit the units between items and the total duration of patterns, respectively ([ 8 ]). By implementing these constraints directly into the generate stage of the ASP solving process, the framework can prune the search space earlier, significantly improving computational efficiency compared to a posteriori testing. Finally, the work provides an extensive empirical evaluation using real-world datasets from network security logs, analysing the time and memory requirements of the grounding and solving phases in various configurations. The problem formulation The CSPM task is built upon the foundations of Sequential Pattern Mining (SPM) ([ 7 ]) and Contrast Pattern Mining (CPM) ([ 3 ]). In this framework, a database $D$ is a multiset of sequences over an alphabet $\Sigma$. A sequence $s$ is considered to be contained within another sequence $t$ (written as $s \subseteq t$) if there exists an embedding, which is a mapping of the items in $s$ to increasing positions within $t$. The support of a sequence $s$ in a dataset $D$, denoted $\textit{supp}(s,D)$, is defined as the number of sequences in $D$ that contain $s$. The goal of CSPM is to identify patterns that differentiate between distinct classes, such as normal versus attack behaviours in the network security domain. This differentiation is quantified using two primary metrics. (1) Given two datasets $D_1$ (class $C_1$) and $D_2$ (class $C_2$), the growth rate (GR) of a pattern $s$ from $D_2$ to $D_1$ is the ratio of its relative support in $D_1$ to its relative support in $D_2$. (2) The contrast rate (CR) is defined as the maximum growth rate across the classes, $\textit{CR}(s) = \textit{max}\{\textit{GR}(C_1),\textit{GR}(C_2)\}$. A sequence $s$ is identified as a contrast sequential pattern if it is frequent (i.e., its support exceeds a minsup threshold) and its contrast rate is at least equal to a user-defined threshold mincr . The ASP formulation The MASS-CSP framework employs ASP to solve the CSPM task using a declarative generate and test principle. The approach is implemented in two distinct phases: First, extracting frequent sequential patterns, and second, verifying which of them meet the contrast requirements. The input database is encoded as ASP facts using the predicates seq(s,p,i) (item i at position p in sequence s ) and cl(s, c) (sequence s belongs to class c ). Candidate patterns are combinatorially generated using choice rules, constrained by minimum and maximum length parameters ( minlen and maxlen ). To determine if a pattern supports a sequence, MASS-CSP utilizes the fill-gaps strategy ([ 6 ]). This strategy is computationally efficient as it focuses only on the leftmost admissible matches of pattern items within a sequence. This ensures that the knowledge of a mapping is maintained for subsequent items, simplifying the search for embeddings. Once frequent patterns are identified, their support is calculated for each class using ASP aggregates. Because standard ASP does not support decimal arithmetic, MASS-CSP integrates external Python functions to calculate growth rates and compare them against the mincr threshold. Integrity constraints then discard any patterns that do not meet the contrast criteria. MASS-CSP extends the basic CSPM task with several advanced modelling features. The framework can find closed and maximal patterns. This is achieved through additional integrity constraints based on the concept of insertable items, ensuring that only the most representative patterns are returned to the user. To improve efficiency and pattern relevance, the gap and span constraints are implemented. Crucially, these are encoded as choice rules within the generate stage rather than as a posteriori tests, allowing the solver to prune the search space earlier and significantly reduce memory and time requirements. Significance of the results By bridging the gap between Pattern Mining and Logic Programming, this research provides a dual contribution that enhances the analytical depth of the former while expanding the practical utility of the latter. Although SPM and CPM are popular pattern mining tasks, their combination (the CSPM task) has received limited attention and lacked a declarative approach. By filling this gap in the existing literature, the research demonstrates that the high-level syntax of ASP is capable of representing the complex metrics of contrast rates and growth rates that characterize this task. The evaluation proves that a declarative approach is not only feasible but also highly effective when complex preferences and restrictions are required. A key finding is that the incorporation of span and gap constraints in the search phase makes the mining process more effective by limiting the search to desired behaviors, which simultaneously decreases execution time and memory requirements. While condensed representations like closed patterns require more computational resources to extract, they successfully reduce the output size, making the results more interpretable for analysts. The significance of the results is further validated by a real-world application in network security. The framework successfully identified attack patterns in 4G-LTE cellular network logs, proving its effectiveness for anomaly detection and intrusion prevention. Furthermore, the declarative nature of the MASS-CSP approach moves the field toward a rich query language for pattern mining, where users can easily adapt the tool to new domains or add new constraints with only a few lines of code. This promotes a level of modularity and ease of maintenance that is difficult to achieve with traditional, specialized procedural algorithms. Relevance to ICLP This work is definitely relevant to the field of Logic Programming, specifically using ASP as a high-level declarative language for problem-solving. ASP is particularly suited for this task because its first-order logic syntax allows for readable and understandable programs that define what a solution is rather than how to compute it. The MASS-CSP approach leverages the generate-and-test principle of ASP to combinatorially generate candidate patterns and then verify if they satisfy specified constraints, such as the minimum support and contrast rate thresholds. The research demonstrates the power of ASP modelling features, such as choice rules for pattern generation, integrity constraints for filtering, and aggregates for calculating the support of patterns. Furthermore, the study addresses the practical challenges of Logic Programming, such as the grounding phase, which can lead to memory explosion if not carefully managed. Using efficient ASP solvers like Clingo, the framework demonstrates that logic-based formalisms can be viable alternatives to specialized procedural algorithms for highly constrained mining tasks. The flexibility of ASP also allows the framework to move toward a rich query language for pattern mining, where users can easily add new constraints with just a few lines of code. ASP-Bench: From Natural Language to Logic Programs Stefan Szeider ( TU Wien ) Answer Set Programming is a declarative approach to knowledge representation and reasoning [ 3 ]. The problem is encoded as a logic program, and the solutions of this program are called answer sets. There exist very efficient solvers such as clingo [ 2 ]. Writing an encoding, however, is a barrier to adoption, as specialist skills and knowledge are required. Therefore, research is focused on translating natural language specifications into logic programs automatically. Language models are well suited for this task. The question remains how to evaluate the encodings produced in this way. ASP-Bench addresses this question. It comprises 128 problem instances: 64 base problems, each in an easy and a hard variant. Easy or hard refers to how difficult the modeling task is expected to be, not how hard the problem is to solve once modeled. The problems contain logic puzzles, graph problems, scheduling, optimization, and constraint satisfaction. ASP-Bench systematically covers core ASP constructs, including basic rules, choice rules, aggregates, and optimization. Every problem has a reference validator, providing the ground truth : a program that checks whether the proposed solution satisfies the specification. This check is independent of how the underlying encoding is written. The evaluation is therefore semantic and not syntactic. The hard problem variants were created by means of planted solutions, by generating a feasible solution first and then adding constraints around it, which guarantees that the instance is solvable. In addition, we made sure that instances have encodings that can be solved within a 20-second time limit. We analyzed the hard variants with respect to seven largely independent aspects: optimization temporal reasoning default logic resource allocation recursion spatial reasoning quantitative complexity Each problem shows between one and six of these aspects. Hence, we can analyze which combinations of aspects make the problem hard to encode. We test the hardness of problems by means of an agentic system that follows the ReAct (Reason and Act) framework [ 6 ]. The agent has access to the clingo Python API. It decides its own actions from the solver feedback, using the error messages and the failed tests to modify the proposed encoding. It does not follow a fixed workflow, in contrast to one-shot or staged-composition approaches [ 4 , 1 ]. The agent is based on Claude Sonnet 4.5. We ran all easy problems twice and all hard problems three times. All runs were successful. We measure the effort in terms of the number of tool calls the agent used. Averaged over three runs, the effort is 7.7 tool calls per hard problem, ranging from 3.7 to 26.0.
